You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Which company do you work for, and what does an ordinary working day look like for you from start to finish?

Interviewee: I work at one of the drone operating companies. My job as a fleet technician is to keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, which involves adding new drones, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can also ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewer: Could you walk me through a typical shift—what do you do first thing when you start, what keeps you busy during the day, and how do you wrap up?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's look at the tasks you mentioned—like taking drones out of service, putting them back, or sending them to charge. How do you find out which drones need your attention?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who hands work over to you, and who do you hand work over to once a drone or charging pad is ready?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day at work, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you check by hand today because you do not trust the current tools or information?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you most afraid a new software service would get wrong?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you add a new drone to the fleet or retire an old one, what information do you have to record or deal with?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When regulators ask to see how your drones have been looked after, what do you have to show them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you set up charging pads at your sites or send drones to charge, what does that involve for you?

Interviewee: I set up our charging pads at our sites, and I also send drones to charge. We have our own charging pads at our sites, a few dozen of them, which use specific charging connectors that are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: What happens if someone tries to send a drone to a charging pad that doesn't have the right connector, or how do you prevent that?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Besides the connector type, what else differs between your drones or your charging pads?

Interviewee: Our drones are of several models from different manufacturers, differing in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. We also have charging equipment and charging pads at our sites, with several connector types in use that are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: How many drones are in your fleet, and how do you keep track of where each one is and whether it is working or in repair?

Interviewee: We run a few hundred drones and a few dozen charging pads at our sites. I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and I also add new drones and retire old ones. I don't know how to keep track of where each one is.

Interviewer: Is there anything else you can tell me about your sites, your repairs, or how your company works with the platform?

Interviewee: Each company runs its own systems, such as billing and customer updates, that need to hear about what happens to its drones and jobs. Our repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after. Each of our sites has a few dozen charging pads, and each drone has a home site.

Interviewer: Can a drone charge or be serviced at a site that is not its home site?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you tell me more about what your company's own systems need to hear about when things happen to your drones?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about your role, the drones, the sites, or the charging equipment that we haven't covered yet?

Interviewee: I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, set up charging pads at our sites, take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge. Our repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians. Regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift to when you go home?

Interviewee: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I plan and run the flights by deciding which drone flies along which way, signing off the flight before it leaves, and potentially calling it off. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I use the service to find out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control like whether the load is ready, the drone reaching its job points, and the drone arriving, while outside people and devices report these things.

Interviewer: How do the jobs reach you at the start of the process, and who do you hand things off to when a flight is done or needs attention?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Where do you see the jobs that need to be planned, and who interacts with your flights before, during, or after you plan them?

Interviewee: I don't know where I see the jobs that need to be planned. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control such as the load being ready or not, the drone reaching the points of its job, and the drone arriving, and these things are reported by people and devices outside the company.

Interviewer: How do you work with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk during the day?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and authorities can announce sudden closures that apply at once or planned ones that are often amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment can deliver an instruction twice while the sender cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

Interviewer: What do you check by hand today because you do not trust the systems or reports you get?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you are deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off on a flight, what specific things do you look at to make sure it is safe and ready?

Interviewee: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way and sign off a flight before it leaves. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.

Interviewer: When you want to find out which of your drones could get to where a job starts, what information do you need to figure that out?

Interviewee: I need to know how much my drones can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. I also need to consider that several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: What else do you need to know about the drone's current state, or the sites and pads it might use, before you pick it for a job?

Interviewee: Each drone has a home site, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

Interviewer: How do you deal with several dispatchers planning at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you most afraid a new service would get wrong?

Interviewee: I worry that a new service would be updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, or that it might occasionally crash. The platform runs on a single server, and the service can suffer interruptions while we are operating.

Interviewer: What happens to your work and your flights in the air when the service crashes or restarts?

Interviewee: I don't know what happens to my work and my flights when the service crashes or restarts. My notes only state that the service runs on a single server, is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes with a few minutes of interruption accepted.

Interviewer: What do you need to know right after something has gone wrong with a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know what I need to know right after something goes wrong.

Interviewer: Earlier you mentioned that a flight is investigated after an accident, or that regulators ask for records—is there anything you or your company need to provide or look at after an incident or when a regulator asks?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens when a sudden airspace closure comes into force while your drones are already in the air, or when a drone's battery drains faster than planned?

Interviewee: I worry when a closure comes into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, or when authorities announce sudden closures that apply at once. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the links used to give instructions to drones are unreliable so an instruction may get through twice while the sender cannot tell if the first arrived.

Interviewer: What makes a job different between parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, or hospital logistics?

Interviewee: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another. Inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started.

Interviewer: What happens if a drone has to travel farther than a single battery charge allows to get to a job or finish a delivery?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you say you want the service to help you find out which of your drones could get to where a job starts, what makes it hard for a drone to get to where a job starts?

Interviewee: I have to account for how far my drones can fly on a full battery, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. I also need to check which sensors they carry, how much they can carry, and which charging connector they use since several types are not interchangeable.

Interviewer: What are all the reasons you might have to call off a flight, either before it leaves or while it is in the air?

Interviewee: I don't know all the reasons I might have to call off a flight. I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I can call off a flight.

Interviewer: Are there any rules from authorities, or rules about the airspace and sites, that you have to follow when deciding which way a drone flies?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you tell me everything else in your notes about airspace, sites, drones, or anything else that affects your work as a dispatcher?

Interviewee: Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, sudden closures that apply at once, and amendments during the day. Radio coverage is patchy, reports from drones can arrive late or out of order, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.

Interviewer: Is there anything else in your notes that we haven't talked about yet?

Interviewee: I know that personal data of staff is covered by the GDPR, and that the platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. None of the companies are seeking certification from the platform, and the relevant rules are the EU drone operation rules and EU U-space rules.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift until you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: To help get us started, what is the very first thing you do when you sit down at the airspace desk in the morning?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Maybe it's easier to think about a specific memorable day—what was the worst day you've had at work in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Who usually hands work to you during a shift, and who do you pass your work along to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there any information or task you currently check by hand because you don't fully trust the existing tools or data?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When something goes wrong in the airspace or with a flight, what is the very first thing you need to know?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Thinking about a new software service being built for your desk, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?

Interviewee: I worry when closures are entered, because I want to know how much disruption was caused across customers. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

Interviewer: When a closure comes into force while drones are already in the air, how do you currently find out which customers and flights are disrupted?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What exactly do you need to know about the disruption across customers when a closure happens?

Interviewee: I want to know how much disruption the closure caused across customers. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

Interviewer: How do you measure or describe "how much disruption" a closure caused—for example, what specific numbers or details are you looking for?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Where do the airspace closures you enter come from, and who sends them to you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are all the steps you take when you enter a closure?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens right after you enter a closure—who needs to know about it, and what do you do next?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Besides entering closures, what other tasks do you handle at the airspace desk?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business, and I work for all customer companies with no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: How do you set up or update the flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When authorities announce a closure, does it apply to specific flight corridors, entire zones, or something else?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Since you have no business looking into any one company's operations or sites, how do you know where the flight corridors between sites should go?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about keeping the shared picture of the airspace, flight corridors, zones, or closures that we haven't covered yet?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. I work for all customer companies and have no business looking into any one company's operations. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
